lesson.grammar_point: obligation and necessity: have to / need to / must (necessary) x don't have to (not necessary) x mustn't (not allowed) -- must + verb without to

listenings.text: I'm a notary public in Florida, and people often think I'm a lawyer. I'm not. My job is simple, but it's important. When you sign a document in front of me, I have to check your ID and watch you sign. You must be there in person, or online with a camera in some states. And please, you mustn't sign the document before you come. If it's already signed, I can't do anything. After you sign, I sign too, and I add my seal. What don't I do? I don't have to read the whole contract, and I can't tell you if it's a good deal. For that, you need to call your lawyer.

Every month, a client asks me the same question: why does this document need an apostille? Here's the short answer. A court in another country doesn't know your notary, so it can't be sure that the signature is real. The apostille is a certificate that says: this signature and this stamp are official. More than a hundred and twenty countries accept it, including Brazil and the United States. That means you don't have to go to an embassy anymore. But there's one rule you have to remember. You have to get the apostille in the country where the document was made. So a Brazilian power of attorney needs a Brazilian apostille, not an American one.

I work as a paralegal in Frankfurt, and half of my job is checklists. When our firm files a claim in another country, every court has its own requirements. Some courts need a certified translation of every page. Others only need the important ones. Some ask for a filing fee, and some don't. So before we submit anything, I make a checklist with three columns: what we have to send, what we don't have to send, and the deadline. My boss used to laugh at my lists. But last year, a missing translation almost cost us a big case. Since then, nobody laughs. Everybody asks for my checklist.
